paragraphs: Hybrid dynamical systems describe processes that combine continuous change with abrupt events. Causal questions about these systems can involve interventions triggered during their evolution, rather than changes imposed only at the beginning. The paper addresses a mismatch: existing causal reasoning frameworks do not adequately support these dynamically triggered, discontinuous interventions, which can make practical analyses difficult to formulate reliably.

The authors define interventions as changes to the constraints governing a hybrid system. This gives counterfactual questions a precise mathematical meaning: how would the system behave under altered constraints? A central complication is that an intervention can leave the modified model without a valid or unique solution. Drawing on hybrid systems theory, the paper identifies mild conditions that preserve solution existence, uniqueness, and measurability.

The framework also expresses established causal quantities within this setting and illustrates probabilities of causation through a fishery-management case study. Its contribution is a foundation for applying causal reasoning to hybrid dynamics while explicitly checking that the intervened system remains mathematically well defined. The guarantees depend on the identified conditions.
neurips-2025-a-counterfactual-semantics-.tldr: The paper formalizes counterfactual interventions in hybrid dynamical systems and identifies conditions under which the resulting models remain well defined.

paragraphs: Finite element simulations divide a physical geometry into a mesh of small elements. Mesh resolution affects both computational cost and accuracy, so placing finer elements where they matter can improve efficiency. Designing that distribution usually requires specialized rules or expert effort. AMBER learns to reconstruct expert mesh choices, turning mesh adaptation into a supervised learning problem.

Starting with a coarse mesh, the method predicts a sizing field: a description of how large mesh elements should be at different locations. An existing mesh generator then uses that prediction to produce an intermediate mesh, and the process repeats. A hierarchical graph neural network makes the predictions. During training, expert labels are automatically projected onto meshes generated by AMBER, supplying guidance for the intermediate states its own procedure creates.

The evaluation covers two- and three-dimensional cases, including physics problems, mechanical parts, and industrial designs with expert meshes. AMBER generalizes to previously unseen geometries and consistently exceeds the tested graph-network, convolutional-network, and reinforcement-learning baselines. These findings support iterative resolution prediction as a practical way to learn adaptive meshing from expert examples.
neurips-2025-amber-adaptive-mesh-generat.tldr: AMBER learns from expert meshes to iteratively predict local element sizes and generate adaptive meshes for unseen geometries.

paragraphs: Difficult reinforcement-learning problems can require searching through many combinations and coordinating multiple agents. Even a system trained until its performance stops improving may produce a limited solution when given just one execution attempt. The paper examines settings where execution allows an additional time and computation budget to explore several attempts before returning a final answer.

The central contribution is to study this inference phase and the strategy used to spend its budget. Training convergence does not necessarily exhaust what a learned system can achieve when additional execution-time exploration is available. In the complex multi-agent problems studied, choosing an inference strategy helps overcome the performance ceiling observed with direct, zero-shot execution.

Across 17 tasks, the authors report improvements over the previous state of the art averaging 45%, with a maximum of 126%, using only a couple of extra seconds during execution. More than 60,000 experiments also show promising behavior as inference computation increases. These findings support treating execution-time strategy as a substantial component of RL performance in applications that permit multiple attempts before committing to a solution.
neurips-2025-breaking-the-performance-ce.tldr: Execution-time inference strategies substantially improve complex multi-agent RL results when applications allow extra computation to explore multiple attempts.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how different attention heads contribute to language-model reasoning. Rather than treating all heads as interchangeable, it asks whether particular heads specialize in functions such as retrieving information or performing logical reasoning. The authors introduce CogQA, a dataset that breaks complex questions into successive subquestions and associates those steps with specific cognitive functions.

A multi-label probing method connects attention-head behavior to these function labels. Across the model families examined, the analysis identifies specialized groups called cognitive heads. The authors characterize these groups as consistently sparse, with their numbers and locations differing across functions. They also find interactions and hierarchical organization, suggesting that the relevant heads have structured relationships rather than acting as isolated components.

The paper goes beyond identifying associations by modifying the cognitive heads. Removing them reduces reasoning performance, while augmenting them improves accuracy in the reported experiments. Together, these findings support their functional importance in the studied models. The framework offers a way to connect internal components with recognizable reasoning operations and suggests directions for model design, training, and fine-tuning.
neurips-2025-cognitive-mirrors-exploring.tldr: CogQA and attention-head analysis reveal sparse functional specializations whose removal or augmentation changes reasoning performance.

paragraphs: Solving a problem alone and reaching a correct answer through discussion require different skills. A useful collaborator must challenge mistakes, explain why a solution is right, and eventually commit to a shared answer. Collaborative Reasoner, or Coral, evaluates these abilities through multi-turn conversations instead of measuring only an individual model's response.

The framework includes six collaborative reasoning tasks spanning coding, mathematics, scientific questions, and social reasoning. Its evaluations find that undesirable social behaviors can make current models fail together even on problems they can solve independently. To improve collaboration, the authors use self-play to generate synthetic conversations with preference information, then train models on that interaction data.

Experiments with Llama-3.1, Ministral, and Qwen-2.5 show consistent improvements over chain-of-thought fine-tuning of the same base models, with gains reaching 16.7 percentage points. Human evaluations also find more effective disagreement and more natural dialogue after training. The results indicate that conversational collaboration benefits from dedicated training objectives: individual reasoning competence does not by itself ensure that a group will use its members' knowledge effectively.
neurips-2025-collaborative-reasoner-self.tldr: Coral uses self-play conversations to train models to disagree constructively, persuade partners, and reach better joint solutions.

paragraphs: Treatment effects can differ between individuals, and an intervention's dose can change its effect on the time until an event occurs. DoseSurv addresses these aspects together. The paper focuses on estimating personalized treatment effects for survival outcomes when treatment choices include both continuously varying doses and options without a dosage component.

The proposed varying-coefficient network uses radial basis functions to represent dose-response relationships continuously. This lets the model express how an estimated response changes as the dose changes. It also learns balanced representations to address covariate shifts in observational time-to-event data. That component targets differences in the characteristics represented across treatment settings, which complicate comparisons of estimated effects.

The authors evaluate DoseSurv across several treatment scenarios using simulated and real-world data and report better performance than existing baseline models. The contribution brings together two problems previously studied largely separately: estimating effects that vary with dosage and estimating effects on event timing. This provides a modeling approach for questions involving which treatment, at what dose, may produce different survival outcomes for different individuals.
neurips-2025-dosesurv-predicting-persona.tldr: DoseSurv combines continuous dose-response modeling and balanced representations to estimate personalized treatment effects on time-to-event outcomes.

paragraphs: Models of molecules and other microscopic systems need to represent geometry while responding consistently when a system rotates. Equivariant graph neural networks provide this capability, but constructing geometric features for graph edges can be expensive. E2Former targets the spherical tensor-product computations that create this bottleneck, particularly when a graph has many connections.

Its main component is a Wigner 6j convolution that moves the relevant computational work from edges to nodes. The stated complexity changes from scaling with the number of edges to scaling with the number of nodes. The authors show that this rearrangement preserves expressive power and rotational equivariance, so the computational savings retain the geometric structure that motivates these models.

The proposed convolution achieves reported speedups of 7–30 times compared with conventional SO(3) convolutions. Experiments with the resulting transformer also show that it captures detailed geometry while reducing computational difficulties. The contribution therefore links an algebraic change in where computation happens to practical efficiency gains, offering a promising direction for scaling molecular models.
neurips-2025-e2former-an-efficient-and-e.tldr: E2Former moves expensive equivariant tensor-product work from graph edges to nodes, preserving geometric expressiveness while accelerating convolution.

paragraphs: Patch-based forecasting divides a time series into short segments so a model can learn from local context and longer-term relationships. Conventional methods use adjacent segments arranged in a fixed way. This paper argues that this fixed representation can restrict the information a forecasting model expresses, and investigates learning which patches to include and how to arrange them.

The Selective Representation Space module combines two learned operations: Selective Patching and Dynamic Reassembly. Together, they adaptively choose and shuffle patches from the available contextual time series. The purpose is to build a representation around informative pieces of the history, making the patch construction itself part of what the model learns.

To test the idea, the authors build SRSNet from the module and a multilayer perceptron prediction head. They report state-of-the-art results on real-world datasets from multiple domains. They also show that the module can improve existing patch-based forecasting models. These findings suggest that better selection and organization of historical segments can meaningfully strengthen forecasting, even with a simple prediction head.
neurips-2025-enhancing-time-series-forec.tldr: SRS learns to select and rearrange time-series patches, improving forecasting in both a simple standalone model and existing patch-based models.

paragraphs: Turning speech into discrete tokens makes it possible to apply language-model-style methods to audio. The difficulty is keeping both what was said and how it sounded while using few bits. Existing codecs can lose semantic or acoustic information, require high bitrates, or rely on multiple codebooks that complicate the models consuming their output.

FocalCodec uses focal modulation networks and a single binary codebook to compress speech at rates between 0.16 and 0.65 kilobits per second. Its design addresses compactness and representational usefulness together. A single codebook provides a simpler token representation while the codec aims to retain information relevant to both linguistic content and the sound of the speech.

The authors report competitive speech resynthesis and voice-conversion performance at lower bitrates than the current state of the art. They also report effective handling of multilingual speech and noisy environments. Downstream evaluations indicate that the representation preserves sufficient semantic and acoustic information and is suitable for generative modeling. These results support compact speech tokenization as a useful interface for several audio tasks.
neurips-2025-focalcodec-low-bitrate-spee.tldr: FocalCodec compresses speech into a single binary codebook at low bitrates while retaining useful semantic and acoustic information.

paragraphs: Image-generation transformers spend substantial computation processing tokens, some of which contain similar information. Token merging reduces that work by grouping similar tokens and replacing each group with a merged representation. This paper examines whether changing the representation used to find those groups can reveal redundancy more effectively and improve generation speed.

Fourier Token Merging transforms token representations into the frequency domain before clustering them. The authors argue that this transformation reduces correlations in a way that helps clustering identify underlying redundancy. The contribution therefore changes how the method recognizes tokens suitable for merging, while retaining the broader goal of sending fewer tokens through transformer computation.

Analytical and empirical studies support the benefits of Fourier-based clustering over clustering in the original representation. In Stable Diffusion experiments, the method reduces latency by up to 25% without impairing image quality in the reported results. The findings show that token-merging efficiency depends partly on the space in which similarity is assessed, making representation choice a useful component of image-generation acceleration.
neurips-2025-fourier-token-merging-under.tldr: Fourier Token Merging clusters tokens in the frequency domain, reducing Stable Diffusion latency by up to 25% without reported image-quality loss.

paragraphs: Game-theoretic algorithms are often tested on recreational games, standard theoretical examples, or randomly generated instances. Security applications introduce more realistic structure, but their evaluation can be hard to reproduce. Even when researchers can reconstruct patrol routes or maps, the data specifying the value of protected targets may remain inaccessible. Those values are central to the incentives the game represents.

GUARD generates two-player matrix and security games from openly available data. It uses animal movements for anti-poaching scenarios and demographic and infrastructure information for protection scenarios. Users can customize utility functions and game parameters or use preconfigured instances. This makes both the physical setting and the incentives more accessible for repeatable algorithm evaluation.

The paper also provides theoretical results on degeneracy and limitations in random-game benchmarking. Its empirical study compares generated games with random baselines using methods for Nash and Stackelberg equilibria, including linear programming, incremental strategy generation, and no-regret self-play. The contribution is an accessible source of realistic benchmark instances together with an analysis of why random instances can provide a limited test.
neurips-2025-guard-constructing-realisti.tldr: GUARD builds customizable game benchmarks from open real-world data and examines the limitations of evaluating algorithms on random games.

paragraphs: Sequence models depend on information in earlier observations that helps predict later ones. Choosing the wrong history length or misreading temporal patterns can therefore undermine generalization. This paper studies predictability as a property of the data itself, using predictive information: the mutual information shared between a sequence's past and its future.

The framework turns that quantity into an information-theoretic learning curve by tracking how much predictive information becomes available as the observation window grows. It extends an earlier idea based on information between the past and only the next observation. Looking at the broader future allows the framework to describe how temporal structure constrains what sequential models can learn.

The theoretical result is an intrinsic information limit: even an optimal predictor cannot exceed the predictive possibilities supplied by the data's patterns. Synthetic-data experiments demonstrate uses for assessing model adequacy, measuring inherent dataset complexity, and identifying interpretable sequence structure. The framework helps distinguish questions about a model's suitability from questions about how much predictive information the sequence contains in the first place.
neurips-2025-how-patterns-dictate-learna.tldr: The paper uses information shared between past and future to characterize intrinsic limits on sequence predictability as observation windows grow.

paragraphs: A forecasting model must do more than produce a plausible prediction: its confidence should also be meaningful. FOReCAst makes both parts of forecasting explicit evaluation targets. The paper identifies shortcomings in existing benchmarks, including narrow question formats, incomplete confidence assessment, and artificial questions that do not adequately reflect practical forecasting needs.

The benchmark covers three kinds of questions: whether an outcome will occur, when it will occur, and what numerical quantity to expect. These formats place different demands on a forecaster. A yes-or-no answer concerns an outcome's occurrence, while a timeframe or quantity prediction requires a more specific estimate. Including all three broadens the forecasting abilities the benchmark can assess.

FOReCAst evaluates prediction accuracy alongside confidence calibration, meaning how well expressed confidence corresponds to prediction reliability. Its stated contribution is this broader evaluation framework across diverse forecasting scenarios. By assessing answers and confidence together, it supports examining whether a model provides useful estimates of its uncertainty as well as accurate predictions for real-world applications.
neurips-2025-introducing-forecast-the-fu.tldr: FOReCAst evaluates forecasting accuracy and confidence calibration across yes-or-no outcomes, timeframe predictions, and quantity estimates.

paragraphs: MOSDT addresses learning safe behavior for multiple agents from an existing dataset. The paper introduces both an algorithm for this setting and MOSDB, a dataset and benchmark intended to make the problem systematically testable. Its design combines policy self-distillation, shared parameters, and an explicit representation of safety-related costs.

The self-distillation method reconstructs global information by fusing observation features from all agents. Full parameter sharing reduces the model's parameter count and stabilizes training; the authors report return improvements of up to 38.4 times from this design. A cost binary embedding module converts cumulative costs into binary safety signals and incorporates those signals into return features, bringing reward and safety information together efficiently.

On MOSDB, which includes environments from MuJoCo, Safety Gym, and Isaac Gym, MOSDT achieves state-of-the-art returns on 14 of 18 tasks while meeting the benchmark's safety requirements completely in the reported evaluation. It uses 65% of the execution parameters of CDT, a state-of-the-art single-agent offline safe RL method. The results connect multi-agent information sharing with stronger returns and efficient execution.
neurips-2025-mosdt-self-distillation-bas.tldr: MOSDT combines shared policies, self-distillation, and cost embeddings to achieve strong multi-agent offline returns with complete safety in its reported benchmark evaluation.

paragraphs: A reasoning model may have a generous thinking budget in one deployment and a tight budget in another. Training only for correctness at the end of a long reasoning trace does not directly reward useful answers at earlier stopping points. AnytimeReasoner trains models to perform well across a distribution of thinking budgets.

The method samples token budgets, truncates a complete thinking process to each budget, and requires the model to summarize an answer from the available reasoning. Verifying those answers supplies rewards at multiple stages, making it easier to assign credit within the reasoning process. The thinking policy and answer-summary policy are optimized separately toward cumulative reward. Budget Relative Policy Optimization adds a variance-reduction technique for training the thinking policy.

Mathematical-reasoning experiments show consistent improvements over GRPO at every tested thinking budget under several prior budget distributions. The authors also report better training and token efficiency. The findings support explicitly rewarding intermediate usefulness when a model must operate under varying computational constraints, rather than judging its reasoning solely by the answer available after a fixed, lengthy process.
neurips-2025-optimizing-anytime-reasonin.tldr: AnytimeReasoner rewards answers at sampled thinking budgets, while BRPO stabilizes training to improve mathematical reasoning across tested budget levels.

paragraphs: When a vision-language model learns from labels supplied by a proprietary teacher, researchers may not know which data or capabilities produced those labels. That obscures the source of progress even when benchmark scores are strong. PerceptionLM studies image and video understanding through a fully open, reproducible framework with visible data, models, and training procedures.

The authors analyze standard training pipelines without distilling from proprietary models and investigate large-scale synthetic data. This analysis identifies important gaps in detailed video understanding. To address them, the project releases 2.8 million human-labeled instances comprising fine-grained video question-answer pairs and captions grounded in both space and time.

The work also introduces PLM–VideoBench, which tests understanding of what happens in a video, where and when it happens, and how it unfolds. Releasing the data, recipes, code, and models makes the training process reproducible and available for inspection. The contribution combines a transparent research foundation with targeted video supervision and evaluation, supporting clearer investigation of detailed visual-understanding capabilities.
neurips-2025-perceptionlm-open-access-da.tldr: PerceptionLM provides open models, training resources, detailed human-labeled video data, and a benchmark for reproducible visual-understanding research.

paragraphs: Forecasting neural activity requires accounting for both an individual neuron's behavior and the activity of the surrounding population. POCO combines these perspectives in one model. It targets cellular-resolution prediction, particularly for spontaneous recordings collected across multiple sessions, an area the paper identifies as less explored than behavioral decoding or interpretability.

The architecture pairs a lightweight forecaster for individual activity traces with an encoder representing population-level dynamics. Training uses five calcium-imaging datasets covering zebrafish, mice, and C. elegans. After pretraining, the model adapts quickly to new recordings with little fine-tuning, supporting its use across recording sessions.

The authors report state-of-the-art forecasting accuracy for spontaneous behaviors in the evaluated data. Learned embeddings for recording units also recover biologically meaningful organization, including brain-region groupings, without anatomical labels. Further analysis identifies context length, session diversity, and preprocessing as important performance factors. These findings connect scalable forecasting with useful learned structure and practical design guidance, while positioning adaptive neurotechnologies and broader neural foundation models as future directions.
neurips-2025-poco-scalable-neural-foreca.tldr: POCO combines individual-neuron forecasting with population context to predict neural activity accurately and adapt rapidly to new recordings.

paragraphs: Prompt tuning adapts a transformer by optimizing a small collection of prompt embeddings. This paper asks how much data those learned prompts can encode, studying exact memorization of finite input-output datasets. The question concerns the expressive capacity of prompt tuning: how prompt length and generation length affect what a fixed-size transformer can represent.

The theoretical analysis gives an upper bound on a sufficient prompt length and establishes a trade-off with the number of autoregressive generation steps. Specifically, a constant-size transformer can memorize n input-output pairs using prompts whose length scales as the square root of n times sequence length, up to logarithmic factors. This is a sufficiency result, rather than a claim that every dataset requires that many prompt positions.

Experiments show that prompt-tuned transformers with randomly initialized backbones can effectively memorize finite datasets. They also capture intrinsic low-rank data structure, reducing the needed prompt length. The authors further study the effect of backbone initialization. Together, the results relate theoretical memorization capacity to empirical behavior and explain how dataset structure can affect prompt efficiency.
neurips-2025-prompt-tuning-transformers-.tldr: The paper bounds sufficient prompt length for dataset memorization and shows how generation steps, data structure, and backbone initialization affect prompt tuning.

paragraphs: A numerical reward indicates how well an action worked, but task descriptions and strategy advice can provide additional guidance. Prompted Policy Search, or ProPS, brings these sources together by putting a language model directly in the reinforcement-learning optimization loop. The model proposes policy updates using both reward feedback and natural-language information.

The paper demonstrates that language models can perform numerical optimization within their context. It then incorporates semantic signals such as goals, constraints, and strategic hints into that process. These signals can guide exploration toward more informed choices and improve learning efficiency. The language model therefore participates directly in deciding how the policy should change.

Evaluation spans 15 Gymnasium tasks from classic control, Atari, and MuJoCo, with comparisons against seven widely used RL algorithms, including PPO, SAC, and TRPO. ProPS beats all compared baselines on eight tasks and shows substantial gains when given domain knowledge. The results support the potential of combining linguistic guidance and numerical feedback, while the reported task coverage shows that superiority is not uniform across the evaluation.
neurips-2025-prompted-policy-search-rein.tldr: ProPS uses a language model to propose policy updates from rewards and language guidance, outperforming all tested baselines on eight of 15 tasks.

paragraphs: Regression trees are useful for nonlinear relationships, interactions, and abrupt changes. This paper instead examines what their fitted structure reveals when the underlying function is smooth and differentiable. It asks whether a tree's node parameters can provide information about the local gradient: how the approximated function changes as its inputs change.

The authors establish a relationship between those parameters and the local gradient, then derive a simple estimate using quantities already exposed by popular tree-learning libraries. The estimate can be computed efficiently. This makes gradient-based analysis available for tree models by estimating properties of the function being approximated.

To demonstrate the approach, the paper considers sensitivity measures involving derivatives and integrals and shows how to calculate them using the proposed gradient estimates. Quantitative and qualitative experiments demonstrate uses in predictive analysis, uncertainty quantification, and interpretation of model behavior. The contribution is especially relevant to the stated smooth-function setting: it extracts local change information from a tree representation and connects that information to tools commonly used with differentiable models.
neurips-2025-regression-trees-know-calcu.tldr: For differentiable target functions, regression-tree parameters provide efficient gradient estimates that support sensitivity analysis, uncertainty quantification, and interpretation.

paragraphs: Matching an object seen from a person's viewpoint with the same object in an external camera view is difficult when viewpoints differ sharply, objects disappear behind obstacles, or targets are small. LM-EEC addresses this correspondence problem using SAM 2 as its foundation. The paper identifies ineffective cross-view feature fusion and limited long-term memory as obstacles when SAM 2 is applied directly.

The proposed framework adds a Memory-View mixture-of-experts module and a dual-memory system. The routing module adaptively weights expert features along both channel and spatial dimensions, helping combine information from different views and memories. The memory banks use compression to retain important long-term information while removing redundancy, addressing the demands of longer videos.

Experiments on EgoExo4D report new state-of-the-art results and substantial improvements over existing methods and the SAM 2 baseline. The authors also report strong generalization across the evaluated scenarios. The results support treating cross-view feature combination and long-term information retention as complementary parts of object correspondence, allowing the model to make better use of evidence distributed across views and time.
neurips-2025-robust-ego-exo-corresponden.tldr: LM-EEC improves first-person-to-external-view object matching by adding adaptive feature routing and compressed long-term memory to SAM 2.

paragraphs: Feature transformation creates new inputs by applying mathematical operations to existing ones. Searching for useful transformations is difficult because the combinations are numerous, while continuous optimization can depend strongly on its starting point and step size. DIFFT approaches the problem as guided generation, learning to produce feature sets suited to a downstream prediction task.

A variational autoencoder first maps feature sets into a compact latent representation. A latent diffusion model generates candidate embeddings in that space, guided by a performance evaluator toward useful transformations. This combines learning the broader distribution of feature representations with task-specific optimization. A semi-autoregressive decoder then converts embeddings into structured, discrete features, maintaining dependencies within each feature while generating different features in parallel.

Across 14 benchmark datasets, the authors report consistent improvements over state-of-the-art baselines in predictive accuracy and robustness, alongside significantly shorter training and inference times. The findings support combining generative exploration, performance guidance, and structured decoding for feature transformation. Each component addresses a different part of the task: exploring candidates, directing them toward predictive value, and turning them into usable features.
neurips-2025-sculpting-features-from-noi.tldr: DIFFT uses performance-guided latent diffusion to generate useful feature transformations, improving accuracy, robustness, and efficiency on 14 benchmark datasets.

paragraphs: Transformer computation can be reduced when only a small subset of neurons and attention connections is active for each token. Reintroducing this sparsity into modern architectures can hurt quality or make training more complicated. Spark Transformer aims to retain model quality, parameter count, and standard training procedures while enforcing sparsity in both feedforward layers and attention.

The architecture uses top-k masking to control how many entries remain active. To avoid the cost of ordinary top-k selection, it introduces statistical top-k, a linear-time approximation designed for accelerators. It also reallocates existing feedforward parameters and attention key embeddings to create an inexpensive predictor of which entries should activate. This helps preserve quality and turn sparse activity into actual runtime savings.

Using the Gemma-2 training recipe, Spark achieves competitive benchmark performance with only 8% of feedforward neurons active and at most 256 attended tokens per token. Reported computation falls by a factor of 2.5. Decoding speedups reach 1.79 times on CPU and 1.40 times on GPU, demonstrating measured runtime benefits as well as reduced arithmetic.
neurips-2025-spark-transformer-reactivat.tldr: Spark Transformer combines efficient top-k selection with activation prediction to make feedforward layers and attention sparse while retaining competitive model quality.

paragraphs: Software-engineering agents need practice on tasks that require interacting with a development environment, running code, and responding to the results. Collections focused on one-shot code generation do not capture that full process, while manually assembled interactive datasets can be small. SWE-rebench introduces an automated pipeline that continuously collects real-world interactive tasks from diverse GitHub repositories.

The pipeline produces a public dataset containing more than 21,000 Python software-engineering tasks, intended to support reinforcement learning at scale. Its continuous collection also serves evaluation. Fresh tasks provide an alternative to repeatedly testing on static benchmarks that may become contaminated as models encounter benchmark-related material during training.

The authors use this supply to construct a benchmark they describe as contamination-free and compare several language models' results with their performance on SWE-bench Verified. The comparison suggests that contamination may inflate some models' scores on the older benchmark. The work therefore connects training-data scale with evaluation freshness: the same collection infrastructure supplies interactive learning tasks and supports a more current assessment of agent capabilities.
neurips-2025-swe-rebench-an-automated-pi.tldr: SWE-rebench automatically collects interactive software-engineering tasks for large-scale training and fresh evaluation that probes possible benchmark contamination.

paragraphs: Cryptanalytic parameter-extraction attacks try to recover a neural network's weights, threatening the investment embodied in its training. This paper introduces a defense aimed at the neuron uniqueness that these attacks need. The approach modifies training so neurons within a layer become less distinguishable in their weight structure.

Specifically, the authors add a regularization term to the usual training loss that reduces distances between neuron weights in the same layer. Because this changes the learned parameters rather than adding inference machinery, the defense has no inference area-delay overhead. The paper also develops a theoretical framework for quantifying an attack's probability of success.

Evaluations across architectures and datasets examine both resistance to extraction and model accuracy. Retraining the same architecture with the modified loss changes accuracy by less than 1% in the reported results. Under prior attack settings, defended networks resist extraction over sustained testing periods, while unprotected networks are extracted within 14 minutes to four hours. These results demonstrate empirical protection against the tested attacks while preserving accuracy closely, rather than establishing unconditional immunity.
neurips-2025-train-to-defend-first-defen.tldr: Extraction-aware training makes neuron weights less distinctive, resisting tested cryptanalytic extraction attacks with less than 1% reported accuracy change.
